articles.title: Roadworks on A664 Manchester Road Scheduled from 7 September 2026
articles.excerpt: Roadworks on A664 Manchester Road in Rochdale will begin on 7 September 2026, affecting traffic flow and access to Bolton Road.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks on A664 Manchester Road will commence on Monday, 7 September 2026, and are expected to last until Friday, 11 September 2026. The works will take place nightly from 8pm to 5am, during which time vehicles will be temporarily prohibited from turning left from A664 Manchester Road onto Bolton Road.

The roadworks are part of ongoing improvements in the area and will affect traffic flow significantly. Drivers are advised to use alternative routes, including A58 Manchester Road northbound, Edinburgh Road southbound, and U-turns at the roundabout, to navigate around the restrictions.

In addition to the A664 Manchester Road works, another set of roadworks is scheduled to begin on Constantine Road from 9 October 2026. This will involve a complete closure of the road for its entire length from 10pm on 9 October until 5am on 10 October, with no alternative route available for vehicles, although access will be maintained for emergency and delivery vehicles.

Local residents and commuters are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly and stay updated on the progress of the roadworks through the Rochdale Borough Council website, where a map of ongoing works across Greater Manchester can also be viewed.

articles.title: Road Closures Announced for Remembrance Sunday Events in Littleborough, Middleton and Milnrow on 8 November 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced temporary road closures for Remembrance Sunday events in Littleborough, Middleton, and Milnrow on 8 November 2026, affecting local traffic and access.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has confirmed that several roads will be temporarily closed on Sunday, 8 November 2026, in Littleborough, Middleton, and Milnrow to facilitate Remembrance Sunday events. The closures are part of the council's arrangements to honour those who have served in the armed forces.

In Littleborough, specific roads will be closed, and waiting will be prohibited in designated areas. Similar measures will be implemented in Middleton and Milnrow, where alternative routes will not be established due to the nature and duration of the events. The council has indicated that the closures are necessary to ensure the safety and smooth operation of the commemorative activities.

Residents and visitors are advised to plan their journeys accordingly, as the road closures may impact local traffic. The council has not specified the exact roads affected in this announcement, but further details can be found on their official website, where a map of the closures will be available closer to the date.

For those wishing to participate in the Remembrance Sunday events, it is recommended to arrive early and consider using public transport where possible. The council encourages community involvement in these important commemorations, which serve to remember and honour the sacrifices made by service members.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Set to Acquire Warwick Mill in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council is preparing to take ownership of Warwick Mill, with a major regeneration announcement for Middleton town centre expected at an event on 7 September.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council is understood to be preparing to take ownership of Warwick Mill, a significant development that could play a central role in the regeneration of Middleton town centre. Although the acquisition has not yet been formally confirmed, further details are anticipated at the 'Our Town, Our Future' event scheduled for Monday, 7 September.

The event, taking place at Middleton Arena, will not only include the announcement regarding Warwick Mill but will also present the results of a consultation involving nearly 2,500 residents and businesses. This consultation is expected to provide valuable insights into community needs and priorities for the area.

In addition to the Warwick Mill announcement, the event will feature updates on the first year of the Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation. Key figures such as Rose Marley and Steve Coogan, co-chairs of the development corporation, will be in attendance, alongside Rochdale Borough Council leader Councillor Neil Emmott and councillors June West and Dylan Williams.

The council was approached for comment regarding the acquisition but did not respond by the time of publication. The developments at Warwick Mill are likely to have significant implications for the future of Middleton, particularly in terms of economic growth and community engagement.

articles.title: Rochdale Residents Urged to Check Voter Registration Ahead of May 2027 Elections
articles.excerpt: With local elections scheduled for May 2027, Rochdale Borough Council is reminding residents to verify their voter registration details to ensure they can participate in upcoming elections.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council is urging residents to check their electoral registration details to avoid losing their chance to vote in the upcoming local elections in May 2027. The council's annual canvass aims to keep the electoral register updated and to identify individuals who may risk losing their voting rights if they are not registered.

Edward McCreadie, elections manager at Rochdale Borough Council, stated that over the summer, emails were sent to residents in more than 40,000 properties, asking them to verify their details. Follow-up letters were dispatched this week, and residents are encouraged to keep an eye out for these communications. McCreadie emphasised the importance of ensuring that the information on the electoral register is accurate and up to date, saying, "To make sure you don’t lose your say at upcoming elections, simply follow the instructions sent to you."

Residents who have recently moved homes are particularly urged to check their registration status. Research from the Electoral Commission indicates that recent movers are less likely to be registered compared to those who have lived at the same address for a longer period. In Great Britain, 92% of individuals who have resided in their homes for 16 years are registered, while only 36% of those who have lived at an address for less than a year are registered.

Individuals aged 16 and above can be added to the electoral register, although they cannot vote until they reach the age of 18. Residents wishing to register can do so easily online at rochdale.gov.uk/RegisterToVote. The council's efforts aim to ensure that all eligible residents can participate in the democratic process during the forthcoming elections.

articles.title: Denehurst House Café Opens in Rochdale, Run by Local Veterans
articles.excerpt: A newly restored café in Denehurst Park, Rochdale, opens on Saturday, 5 September 2026, managed by a local veterans' organisation and offering a community space.
articles.content_html:
A 19th century manor house in Rochdale, which has been vacant for decades, has been transformed into a café that will officially open on Saturday, 5 September 2026. Located in Denehurst Park, the café occupies the ground floor of Denehurst House and aims to provide a welcoming space for the community.

The café will be managed by the local Community Interest Company, Get Together After Serving (GTAS), which is staffed entirely by former armed forces personnel and their families. GTAS was established by Rochdale residents Adam Trennery, Wayne Traynor, and Wayne Simms, with the goal of supporting the local veteran community through various wellbeing programmes and events.

Visitors to the café can expect a menu featuring hot and cold sandwiches, cakes, breakfasts, and a selection of teas and coffees. The café will also collaborate with local businesses to offer special menu items on Fridays, including curries, pizzas, and pies. Additionally, the venue is designed to serve as a gathering place for local veterans.

The restoration of Denehurst House was commissioned by Rochdale Borough Council, which worked with local builders H Bell and Sons and interior design specialists to preserve the building's period features, such as ornate coving and bay windows. The council plans to use the remainder of the building to provide accommodation for local veterans, following a recent public consultation on this proposal.

articles.title: Horse in Rochdale left critically ill after being fed harmful food by campers
articles.excerpt: A horse owner in Rochdale is seeking awareness after her horse, Frank, fell critically ill due to being fed harmful scraps by campers. The incident has raised concerns about the dangers of feeding horses human food.
articles.content_html:
A horse in Rochdale has been left in a critical condition after being fed something dangerous by campers, according to his owner, Julie Kershaw. The incident occurred when Julie, 58, discovered her 13-year-old horse, Frank, trembling and unable to walk in the field where he is kept. Julie believes that the campers fed Frank human food, which led to his distress and subsequent health issues.

Julie was alerted to Frank's condition by her daughter, who was out walking with a friend when they found the horse shaking uncontrollably and struggling to breathe. They quickly issued a Facebook appeal to locate Julie, who rushed to the scene. Upon arrival, she found Frank in a dire state, fearing he would not survive the night. Julie stated, "He was really shaking and couldn't walk," highlighting the severity of the situation.

A vet was called and arrived within 40 minutes, administering four injections to treat Frank's condition, which was diagnosed as colitis, an infection in the colon. The emergency visit resulted in a vet bill of £235, with additional costs for food bringing the total to around £300. Julie expressed her frustration, stating, "It's just so scary - people don't realise how dangerous it is to feed horses."

This incident is not isolated; Julie noted that horse owners in the area have previously found harmful items such as chicken bones and vegetables discarded in fields. She urged the public to educate themselves on what is safe to feed horses, emphasising that even common treats can become dangerous if overfed. Julie's experience serves as a reminder of the potential risks associated with feeding horses human food.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real, water‑carved nook of rock that has gathered centuries of stories — but folklore and documentary record tell very different tales.
articles.summary: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real, water‑carved nook of rock that has gathered centuries of stories — but folklore and documentary record tell very different tales.
articles.body:
Walk under the stone viaduct at Healey Dell and you’ll find a narrow cleft where the River Spodden thunders through a rocky throat. Local signs and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre point visitors to a spot long called the Fairies’ Chapel — an evocative name that has attracted guidebooks, children’s trails and Victorian collectors of legend alike. The site is part of Healey Dell Nature Reserve, managed and promoted by Rochdale Borough Council as a place of industrial archaeology, woodland and waterfalls. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What is indisputable: the place and its industrial history are real. The high stone viaduct that dominates the valley is a Grade II‑listed Victorian structure on the National Heritage List for England, and the valley contains the remains of mills, lodges and a former railway line now used as a trail. These are documented, protected features and form the historic backdrop that helped foreground the rock seat and grotto known as the Fairies’ Chapel. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

What created the ‘chapel’ is ordinary geology and the work of water. Guides and local interpretation explain that the Thrutch — a narrow gorge — contains a small natural excavation scored by the attrition of the river; older accounts and the Healey Dell visitor material say a great flood in early July 1838 altered or destroyed some of the rock formations formerly seen there. In short: the chapel‑like shapes are the result of erosion and historic landscape change, not built masonry. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

And the fairies? That is the realm of story. The best‑known accounts of the Fairies’ Chapel come from 19th‑century collectors such as John Roby, whose Traditions of Lancashire (first published in 1829 and reprinted in later nineteenth‑century editions) recorded a long narrative about a miller, a Lady Eleanor, a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden, and encounters with fairy royalty in the Thrutch. Roby’s work, and later local retellings and guidebook extracts, mixed oral tradition, local gossip and romantic reconstruction — material to be enjoyed as folklore, not read as factual history. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Versions of the tale vary. In some tellings a Fairy King condemns witches to a rocky chapel; in others a prophecy or an enchanted hare leads a boastful miller into the fairy grotto. These stories have been printed and reworked for more than a century, and they fed Victorian visitors’ appetite for “haunted” beauty spots. The modern Healey Dell Heritage Centre preserves and retells many of these legends, and the valley’s trails now include family‑friendly interpretation such as a fairy grotto for children. Those activities keep the stories alive, but do not serve as evidence that supernatural beings live there. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

So: are there really fairies in Healey Dell? If you mean literal, sentient fairies as found in the stories — no contemporary, verifiable evidence supports that claim. If you mean “are there stories, traditions and a long local appetite for the uncanny” — absolutely. The Fairies’ Chapel is a genuine landscape feature with a documented industrial and geological history; it is also a cultural site where folklore collected since the early 19th century continues to be told and enjoyed. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

For visitors: treat the site as a meeting of nature, history and imagination. Respect the reserve’s paths and signage, enjoy the viaduct and waterfalls documented by Historic England and the borough, and bring a good torch if you try the narrow paths near the Thrutch. Above all, enjoy the stories as stories — valuable for what they tell us about local memory and the way places gather meaning over time. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

articles.title: Elite Hand Car Wash in Rochdale Fined for Minimum Wage Violations
articles.excerpt: Elite Hand Car Wash on Molesworth Street has been penalised for failing to pay a worker the minimum wage, as part of a government initiative naming over 600 employers.
articles.content_html:
Elite Hand Car Wash, located on Molesworth Street in Rochdale, has been penalised for failing to pay a worker the national minimum wage. The business, operated by Ms Misbah Khalil, is among 658 employers recently named by the government for similar violations.

The government initiative revealed that Elite Hand Car Wash owed £4,590.40 to one employee. This is part of a broader effort that has seen nearly £4 million returned to over 27,000 workers across the UK who were underpaid. Additionally, employers have faced penalties totalling £7 million for non-compliance with wage regulations.

The current national minimum wage is set at £12.71 per hour for workers aged 21 and over, £10.85 for those aged 18 to 20, and £8 for under-18s and apprentices. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds emphasised the importance of treating workers fairly, stating that responsible businesses understand that looking after their employees is essential for success.

As a result of this naming and shaming initiative, Elite Hand Car Wash may face increased scrutiny from both the public and regulatory bodies. Local residents and potential customers may wish to consider this information when choosing services in the area.

articles.title: Rochdale Sees Rise in Teenagers Seeking Treatment for Addiction
articles.excerpt: More than 170 teenagers in Rochdale received treatment for alcohol and drug abuse, highlighting a growing demand for addiction services in the borough.
articles.content_html:
More than 170 teenagers in Rochdale received treatment for alcohol and drug abuse in the past year, reflecting a significant rise in demand for addiction services among young people and adults. This increase comes as the borough's Health, Schools and Care Overview and Scrutiny Committee prepares to meet on Wednesday to discuss strategies for addressing addiction issues, including tobacco, vaping, drugs, alcohol, and gambling.

In a report to the committee, Kuiama Thompson, Director of Public Health and Communities, stated that drug and alcohol harm continues to significantly impact the health of Rochdale residents. This includes avoidable hospital admissions and premature mortality, which place additional pressure on health and care services and exacerbate health inequalities. The report also noted the broader societal impacts of addiction, such as increased safeguarding concerns, crime, homelessness, and unemployment.

According to figures from the National Drug Treatment Monitoring System, there are approximately 1,831 individuals in Rochdale who use opiates and crack cocaine, alongside 2,905 individuals with alcohol dependency. While there is no evidence of an overall increase in alcohol consumption in the borough, the harm caused by long-term heavy drinking is on the rise, likely due to historical drinking patterns and socio-economic deprivation.

The main substances leading young people to seek treatment include cannabis and alcohol. Ms Thompson highlighted that strong pathways have been established to identify young people presenting with health issues who may not disclose their drug use, ensuring they receive the necessary support.

articles.title: Rochdale's Year as Town of Culture Generates Over £5.5 Million for Local Economy
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's designation as Greater Manchester's Town of Culture has resulted in a significant economic boost, with over £5.5 million generated from nearly 300 events throughout the year.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's year as Greater Manchester's Town of Culture has brought in more than £5.5 million for the local economy, according to a report from Rochdale Council. The evaluation, which assessed the value for money of the Town of Culture status, revealed that the borough attracted 213,099 attendees across 297 events during the 2025/2026 year.

The council's figures estimate that the economic impact was based on a conservative spending estimate of £25 per person. However, an assessment by Marketing Manchester suggested that the actual boost could be as high as £16.6 million, based on a daily visitor spend of £78. The council received £50,000 from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) Culture Fund to support cultural activities from April 2025 to March 2026, indicating that the Town of Culture initiative was a worthwhile investment.

The local authority collaborated with the Rochdale Development Agency (RDA) and various partners to deliver a diverse range of cultural events, including 'The Herds', Street Eat, Rochdale Comedy Festival, Rochdale Pride, and the Ignite Fire Festival. The report also highlighted significant advertising investments and increased opportunities for local artists and freelancers, contributing to a vibrant cultural scene.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation, expressed pride in the success of the initiative, noting that 94% of attendees felt the events enhanced Rochdale's image. She emphasised the importance of culture in fostering community engagement and representation, and stated that the momentum created during this year would pave the way for future cultural investments and events in the borough.

Greater Manchester Police seized six high-performance vehicles in Rochdale as part of a crackdown on anti-social driving, following reports of dangerous behaviour on the M66.

Officers from Greater Manchester Police’s Transport Policing and Crime Command (TPACC) seized six luxury cars in Rochdale last night as part of a crackdown on anti-social and dangerous driving. The operation followed reports of reckless driving involving high-powered vehicles, including Lamborghinis and Mercedes G-Wagons, on the M66.

Witnesses reported that the vehicles were being driven at excessive speeds, weaving across lanes, and performing wheel spins, with some slowing down to speeds as low as 17mph on the motorway. Police located the convoy on the M62 and successfully stopped two Lamborghinis as they exited the motorway. The remaining vehicles were brought to a halt using specialist tactics in Rochdale.

Five Lamborghinis and one Mercedes G-Wagon were seized under Section 59 of the Police Reform Act 2002. In addition to the vehicle seizures, the drivers of the offending vehicles are facing prosecution for multiple driving offences.

Chief Inspector Danny Kabal of GMP’s TPACC stated, “We take road safety very seriously in GMP, and we will not tolerate careless, inconsiderate, anti-social or dangerous driving on our roads.” This operation highlights the police's commitment to ensuring safety on local roads and addressing the concerns of residents regarding reckless driving.

articles.excerpt: The family of Michael Hoolickin, murdered in Middleton in 2016, has welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for accountability regarding failures in the probation system that contributed to his death.

The family of Michael Hoolickin, murdered in 2016, has welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for accountability regarding the probation system that failed to protect him. They advocate for reform and a formal apology from the government.

The family of Michael Hoolickin, a 27-year-old father murdered in Middleton in 2016, has expressed support for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent call for accountability concerning the probation system's failures that contributed to his death. Michael was killed by an offender who had a history of violent crime and had been under probation supervision despite numerous breaches of his licence.

Michael Hoolickin was stabbed outside the Friendship Inn on Cheapside on October 14, 2016, by an individual who had previously been jailed for violent offences, including biting off a man's ear. Despite over 50 breaches of probation conditions, including positive drug tests and arrests, the offender remained free until the fatal incident. Michael's parents, Garry and Lesley Hoolickin, have since campaigned for reforms in the Probation Service and co-founded the campaign group VOICE (Victims Oversight In Criminal Enforcement).

During a recent parliamentary session, Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell highlighted the Hoolickin family's plight, stating that Michael's murder was a result of the inadequate monitoring of violent offenders by the Probation Service. The family is advocating for a formal apology from the government to families affected by similar tragedies and is calling for a comprehensive review of the probation system, which statistics indicate has led to one victim every three days.

The Prime Minister's acknowledgment of the Hoolickin case and the broader issues within the probation system may lead to significant discussions about reform. The family hopes that increased scrutiny will prevent future tragedies and ensure that offenders are held accountable for their actions.

articles.title: Medieval Knights to Compete in Full-Contact Combat at The Ashcroft in Whitworth
articles.excerpt: The Ashcroft in Whitworth will host Saturday Knight Fights 6 on September 26, featuring full-contact Medieval combat in an MMA-style cage.
articles.content_html:
Medieval knights will return to Whitworth this month for Saturday Knight Fights 6, an event showcasing full-contact Medieval combat. The competition will take place at The Ashcroft on Saturday, September 26, and is presented by Honour and Arms HMB Ltd, a local club dedicated to the study and competition of historical fighting.

The event promises an evening of excitement as knights clad in full armour engage in battles within an MMA-style cage. Daniel and Mary George, who own and operate Honour and Arms, emphasised the thrilling nature of the fights, stating, "We keep the action rocking and rolling with Saturday Knight Fights 6. Join us for an evening filled with excitement and adrenaline as fighters go head to head in the cage."

Honour and Arms offers workshops and courses on various styles of historical fencing and European martial arts, catering to both beginners and experienced practitioners. The club aims to promote the sport and provide opportunities for enthusiasts to engage in full-contact Medieval combat.

Local residents and visitors are encouraged to attend the event, which is likely to attract a diverse audience interested in historical combat sports. Further details about the event can be found on the Honour and Arms website.
